about: The words of the chain house_new_ship (Data/encounters/chain_house_new_ship_793.json; Design/content/chains/house_new_ship.md): a bigger ship built over a winter at Dorestad's dam heads. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the six news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: nobody is named in the words. The count is the spine's Folcbert in his years and the moneyer the spine's Sigimar; the wright, the steward, the smith, the weaver, the Dane, the priest and the river wright are ordinary invented people whom the forge names. Nothing is quoted from a translation: s10.riddle is Symphosius 13 (Navis; texts_793.json symphosius_13_navis, Riese 1894) and s10.bless follows the old blessing of a ship that names Noah's ark, both in our own plain rendering; s02.moon gives Vegetius IV.35-36 in a steward's words; the Sunday rule in s05 and s08 is the Admonitio generalis of 789 in a weaver's and a wright's words. Written 6 Oct 2026 over the cards of 4 Oct; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: A keel on the sand
The wright at the dam heads has no hull on his slip. He has watched your boat come and go all summer, and he has an opinion about her.
Your boat goes out so deep that the eels look over the rail. A house that loads like that has outgrown four oars.
You went away to think. Thinking is cheap, and my slip has stood empty the whole time you were at it.
A keel ship. Thirty-four feet of keel, forty-six over the stems, a hold for six times what you carry now, and five men to work her.
A pound of pennies now, so I keep the slip for you. Ordered by Martinmas, afloat by Easter. A pound and a quarter more on the day she swims.
You find the stuff. Fourteen oaks from up the Rhine, with the crooked boughs left on. Ten kegs of rivets. A sail from the terp women. I find the hands.

He cuts a hazel stick to the length of his forearm and notches it three times: the width of a plank, the thickness of a rivet's shank, the span between rivets. The stick is the ship, he says. Do not lose it.
They say you owe the Wōkerer. That is between you and him, until he makes it my business.
Count out a pound of pennies as earnest
Offer half a pound and your name
Ask what it will all cost, and go away to think

He counts the pennies twice, by twelves, and puts the stick in your hand. By evening two posts stand in the sand where her stems will be. You have ordered a ship: oak from Colonia, iron from Daventre, a sail from Wijnaldum.
He weighs the half pound in his hand and your name in his head, and takes both. The stick is yours. He says he has built for worse payers, and that most of them paid.

He reckons it on his fingers: the earnest, the oak, the iron, the sail, his wage at the launch. Near five pounds of silver, if nothing goes wrong. He says something always goes wrong. He will ask again while the summer lasts.
Oak across the river
Across the river from the city stand the old fort and the king's estate, and behind them the king's wood. The steward walks you through the oaks with the wright's stick in your hand.
The king wants his woods kept and his clearings cleared. This is a clearing. Every oak you take out of it is one I need not burn.
We fell after midsummer and before Christmas, and when the moon is past her full. A Roman wrote that in a book about war. I have not read it. The oaks seem to have.
Felled, limbed and bound with withies into a raft. Six days down to your dam heads with two of my men on it. They walk home, so feed them well.
Or take what the storm took two winters ago. It lies there dry, and I will sell it for less than half. A wright will tell you why.
I have trees and no axes. Every man who can lift one has gone into Saxony with the king, again. If your crew can swing, they can earn your oak.
My men are home from Saxony and tired of it. If your crew will swing axes in their place for a few weeks, you can earn your oak instead of buying it.
And there is that one. Four men cannot ring it with their arms. Too great to cleave for planks. Hollowed and spread, it is a river ship by itself, and no iron in her.
Buy fourteen standing oaks and the crooked boughs
Take the windfalls: dry, and cheap
Lend your crew to the clearing and take the pay in oak
Buy the great oak and have a river ship made of it here
The steward cuts his mark and yours into fourteen trunks. They will fall when the moon allows and come down on the river. The raft should lie at Dorestad in fifty days.

The windfalls are grey and hard as horn, and they ring when struck. They are bound into a raft within the week. The steward takes your silver and wishes your wright patience. The raft should lie at Dorestad in twenty-five days.

Your men fell oaks for the king for three weeks and curse you for all of them. No silver changes hands. Their hands are raw and the steward has learned their names. The raft should lie at Dorestad in sixty-five days.

You buy the one great oak. A wright of the river bank will hollow it here, through the winter, with fire and adze. The stick in your hand is no use now, and the wright at Dorestad keeps your earnest. Come back in a hundred days.
The raft at the dam head
The raft lies against your dam, low in the water, with a Frank asleep on it. The wright walks its length, strikes each trunk with the back of his axe and listens.
Good oak, and wet, as it should be. Eleven of these will cleave true. Three have a twist in the grain that I cannot wedge out.
This is dead wood. It will blunt every axe I own and split wherever I put a rivet. And three of them are twisted as well.
There is an old keel ship sunk at her post by the north dams. Nobody has claimed her since my father's day. Her knees and floors are grown oak, and sound under the mud.

His men drive wedges into the first trunk. It opens along its length with a sound like ice going on the river, and the two halves lie steaming in the cold. Nobody here owns a saw long enough, or wants one.
So. Three more oaks from upriver, or the old ship's bones, or I build with what came. I will do any of the three. Only one of them will I do without saying so afterwards.
Send upriver for three more oaks
Raise the old ship's knees and floors from the north harbour
Tell him to build with what came

The Frank wakes, takes sixty pennies and the wright's message, and walks south. Three more trunks will come down behind a wine boat. The keel is laid meanwhile, on blocks, with its scarf to the river. The wright wants thirty days before he will talk about her shape.

Your men spend four days to the waist in cold mud at the north dams. Nine knees and six floor timbers come up black and whole. What is left of her settles deeper. The keel is laid. The wright wants twenty days before he will talk about her shape.

The wright looks at you for a while and then at the twisted trunks, and tells his men to cleave them. The keel is laid. He says nothing more that day, and wants twenty days before he will talk about her shape.
Iron from the heath
West of the river the heath smokes day and night. Its iron comes down to the bank at Daventre. The smith takes the wright's stick and turns it over in his fingers.
Brown stones off the heath, and charcoal, and three days of a man's breath. It is soft iron. It bends before it breaks, which is what you want between two planks.
A ship of this notch is two thousand rivets, each with its rove. Ten kegs. A man can carry one keg and will tell you about it afterwards.
Every wright from here to the sea sends me a stick. Yours is the first this year with the notches cut square. He knows what he is about.
The emperor has ordered ships built on every river. His men take iron at their own price and call it service. What I sell you, I sell you today.
My blooms lie at the furnaces, a day's walk into the heath. Carry them down for a week with your crew and I take half the price.
Buy ten kegs cut to the wright's notch
Carry his blooms down from the heath for a week, and pay half
Buy nothing today

He tries a rivet from each keg against the notch before he lets it go. Ten kegs go into your hold, and she sits down in the water under them. They are for the wright at Dorestad when he asks for iron.

A week on the heath with a yoke on your shoulders. The furnace men live in the smoke and laugh at shipmen. Ten kegs for half the silver, and a smith who now calls you by name. They are for the wright at Dorestad when he asks for iron.
He hands the stick back and goes on with his work. The iron will be here next time. He does not promise the price will.
The weavers of the terp
On the terp the looms stand in huts dug half into the ground, where the damp keeps the warp from snapping. The woman who speaks for the weavers hears what you want and looks at her hands.
A sail that size is four women and a winter. You have come at the right end of the year. The looms are warm and there is nothing else to do but talk.
A sail that size is four women and a winter, and you ask in summer, with the sheep to shear and the hay to get in. It will be woven. It will take the same days.
And count six days to the week. The king has sent word that women shall not weave on the Lord's day, nor card, nor shear. He did not say who spins his own cloaks.
Our law prices a weaver's hand with a harper's and a goldsmith's. Break into a weaving hut and you pay with your neck. Remember that when you come to haggle.
Silver is well enough. But a mound in the salt marsh has no stone, no vines and no trees. Good querns and a cask of wine say more here than pennies.
Or take cloak-cloth off the bench today and have it sewn. It is woven for backs, not for wind. It will stretch like a wet stocking, but it is there.
Order the sail: half the silver now, half when it is woven
Pay the first half in quernstones and wine
Buy the cloak-cloth and have it sewn for a sail
Not yet
She takes ninety pennies and ties a knot in a red thread for each of them. The long wool is set aside for you. Come back in a hundred and ten days with the other half.

Two black querns go up the terp on a sledge with half the village behind them, and the cask after. Nobody mentions silver again. The long wool is set aside for you. Come back in a hundred and ten days with the other half.
The cloak-cloth is sewn into a sail in two days by every woman who can hold a needle. It is a handsome blue. The weavers do not say what they think of it, and you have a sail aboard.
She nods and goes back into the hut. A loom does not care when you come, she says, only how long you leave it alone.
Off the looms
The sail lies folded on a bench in the largest hut: fifteen lengths sewn edge to edge, grey as a seal and heavier than a man. It smells of sheep and smoke.
Fifteen lengths, each as long as your mast is tall. The fleeces of a hundred sheep, and only the long outer wool. Count the seams if you like. We did.
Your querns grind fine and the wine was drunk at a wedding. The bride's mother wove the middle length. You may think it the tightest.
A shipman of Dorestad was here at the new moon, one with a dam head of his own. He offered half as much again for it as it lay. I told him it was spoken for. He laughed.
Rub it with mutton fat and red earth before it meets the wind, or the wind will go straight through it. That part is your work.
Pay the second half, as agreed
Pay it, and match the other man's offer as a gift
Say the edge is thin, and offer two thirds
Leave it on the bench until you have the silver
She unties the knots in the red thread one by one as you count. Four men carry the sail down to the boat. It is the terp's own weave, and the wright will know it.

You pay what was agreed and lay the other man's offer on top of it, and say it is for the women. She is silent, which on the terp is praise. The cloaks will be cheap for you this season, and they want four casks of wine and will pay over the price.
You hold the edge to the light and say what you see. She sees it too. She takes two thirds and has the sail carried down, and nobody helps your men lift it aboard.

She folds the sail away from under your hand. It was spoken for, she says, and now it is spoken for again. The shipman of Dorestad has it by the next tide. You will have to find a sail elsewhere, or launch under the old one.
The sail stays on the bench with a clean fleece over it. She will keep it twenty days more. She does not say what happens after that.
The Dane's opinion
The keel and both stems are up and the first strakes are on. A Dane off a Ripa ship that winters at the dam heads has stood before her every morning for a week. Today he speaks.
It is a good trough. My father built ships. He would take two fingers off every plank, a foot off her depth, and give her sixteen oars.
And she would carry four tons where mine carries six, and want twelve men fed where mine wants five. I build for merchants. They count.
Yours carries more. Mine arrives. She goes against the wind on her oars, up any creek, and nothing with a sail alone will catch her.
A ship of that look on this river, with their king and his fleet sitting at Sliesthorp? The count's men will board her first and ask whose she is afterwards.
Your own Northman has come up behind you. He looks along the keel, then at the Dane, and says one word in their tongue. The Dane nods. It was the word for fast.
Choose today. From here on every plank is cut for the one ship or the other. And whichever she is, I want the iron within sixty days, or I go looking for old.
Keep the wright's ship: deep and broad, built to carry
Let the Dane line her off: lighter, lower, more oars
Ask the wright, before his men, what he would take from the Dane

The wright does not smile, but he sends a boy for ale. The Dane lifts one shoulder and goes back to his ship. She will be deep and broad, as she was drawn in the sand. The planking goes on for twenty-five days before he needs the iron.

You give the Dane forty pennies and a chalked line. He walks her length, laying it along the stems, and the wright's men watch their master. The wright says he has built to worse orders. She will be long and low. The planking goes on for twenty-five days before he needs the iron.

The wright thinks, before all his men, and it costs him something. Then: the Dane's way with the top strake, and nothing else. The Dane grins and gives you a riddle of his people for your trouble. She stays the wright's ship. The planking goes on for twenty-five days.

The wright says he would take the Dane's ale and nothing more, and his men laugh too loudly. He does not thank you for asking where they could hear. She stays his ship. The planking goes on for twenty-five days.
The wright will not be hurried
Four strakes a side, and the wright has stopped. He needs the iron now, and you need to know when she will swim. He answers the second question first.
Ninety days, if the frost lets the tar run. Ask me again tomorrow and it is ninety-one.
Ninety days from the day I have the iron. It is not winter, so the men will want to be in the fields, and I will not stop them. Ninety.
Green oak moves as it dries. Rivet it too fast and it tears itself round the iron. I put on a strake, and then I let her think about it.
And today is a feast. There is not a hammer lifted on these dams today, and you are the only man here who has noticed.
No Sundays. The king forbids it, the priest watches the dams from his door, and our own law fines a free man for it. I am a free man.
Your dry oak splits at every third rivet. I bore each hole twice as slowly, and it still splits. I said it would.
The Dane's planks are two fingers thinner than mine. One slip of the axe and the plank is firewood. My men are learning. I am not paying for the lessons.
And you have come without the ten kegs. Then it is the breaking beach, and old rivets cut out of dead ships. Iron remembers every hole it has been in.
Hand over the ten kegs and let him keep his own pace
Hand over the iron and pay for four more men of his choosing
Hand over the iron and tell him to work feast days and by torchlight
Bring no iron: let him cut old rivets on the breaking beach
He has the kegs rolled under the hull and opens one with his own hands. Ninety days, he says again, as if you had argued. She will be ready for the rollers then.
He picks four men off the dams by looking at their hands, not their faces. With ten at the planks she will be ready in sixty days. He does not call it hurrying. He calls it more men.

They work by torchlight and through two feasts, with a boy set to watch the church door. Nobody tells the priest. She will be on the rollers in thirty days. The wright has stopped looking at her seams when you are near.

They work by torchlight and through two feasts. Somebody tells the priest. The fine is twelve pennies and it is yours, read out at the church door. She will be on the rollers in thirty days. The wright has stopped looking at her seams when you are near.

His boys spend a week on the breaking beach with cold chisels, cutting rivets out of dead planks and beating them straight. They are a hundred shapes of brown. She will be ready in ninety days, the wright says, and he does not say for what.
The count at the slip
The count has ridden down to the dam heads with his steward and stands before the hull with his thumbs in his belt. The wright's men have all found work at the far end of her.
So this is where my silver went. A man who owes me builds himself a ship. I have not decided whether that is impudence or good sense.
You owe me nothing, and here you are with a ship on my bank. I like to see it. I like still more to know whose she is.
The king wants boats in Saxony. He has them dragged over dry land from river to river, and he asks his counts where the boats are to come from.
The king has set ships and watchmen at every river mouth against the heathen men. I am to find hulls for this one. I have found one.
The emperor has ordered a fleet built on every river that runs to this sea, and means to come and look at it himself. Every count is counting keels.
The coast must be watched, whoever is emperor. Ships are ordered and ships are not built, and then a count is asked why.

Give her to me for the king's service. I count back all you have laid out, you have a plot at the dam heads, and my hand is over your house. Or carry for me once a year. Or say no. I have heard the word before.
Say she is the house's ship, with respect
Offer one carrying a year at the count's word, for an easier toll
Offer the carrying for a year's delay of the Wōkerer's day
Give her to the count for the king's service
The count looks at the hull a little longer than is comfortable, and says a house should have a ship. He rides back up to the hall. The wright's men come back along the hull one by one.
One carrying a year, when his steward sends: the count's corn, or the count's men. He has it said before witnesses. The toll man will take half from you for half a year. The ship is still yours.
One carrying a year, and for it the Wōkerer's day is put off a year. He cuts a new notch in the tally and does not look pleased to. The ship is still yours.

You give her, there on the sand, before she has touched water. The count's steward counts back nine hundred pennies and paces out a plot at the dam heads. The wright finishes her for the king. You are the count's shipman now, and the toll man knows it.
The launching
She stands tarred black on the slip with her stem to the river. Tallowed rollers lie under her keel, a rope runs to every hand on the dam, and the priest of the upper church has brought his book.
She will weep for a day or two while the oak drinks. Then she will take up and be tight. Do not bail her dry in a fright. Let her drink.
I have put right what could be put right. She is a sound ship. She is not the ship she could have been, and only you and I will ever know it.
Lord, who bade Noah build of wood and carried eight souls over the flood, stretch out your hand over this ship and over those who go in her, and bring them to the harbour they wish for.

My master set us this at school. Long and swift I go, daughter of a fair forest, with a great company crowded close about me. I run many roads and leave no footprint. I never guessed it. I was born inland.
I have cut my mark under her stem, where the water will hide it. I do not do that for every hull.
Your old boat lies at the next post with her four oars shipped. From up here she looks like something the new ship might carry on deck.
Bend on the terp sail, pay the wright and send her down the rollers
Pay the wright and launch her under the sailcloth you have
Pay the wright and launch her under the old boat's sail
Not yet: leave her on the slip

She goes down the rollers faster than anyone meant and sits on the river as if she had always been there. The grey sail goes up and fills. The wright says you may build on your own dam from now on, and he will come to you. The priest gives you his tablet with the riddle on it. Everyone on the dams wants tar.

She goes down the rollers and takes the water with a sound like a long breath. The sail is not the one she was drawn for, and she swims well under it all the same. The priest gives you his tablet with the riddle on it. The house has a keel ship.

She goes down the rollers and floats high and handsome. The old boat's sail on her yard looks like a child's shirt on a carter. She will be slow until she has a sail of her own. But she swims, and she is the house's.
The ropes are coiled again and the priest takes his book home. The wright says a ship keeps on a slip. He also says tallow does not.
A ship before her time
She stands on the rollers, tarred, and to any eye but one she is a ship. The wright has not cut his mark under her stem, and says he will not.
Dead oak. There are splits at the rivets under that tar. I have stopped them with wool and they are still splits.
Three strakes are of the twisted trunks. They sit against their neighbours like a bad marriage. I have made them lie. I cannot make them like it.
Half her rivets came out of dead ships. Some will hold for twenty years. Some for two. They all look alike.
And that sail is a cloak. In the first hard blow it will stretch into a bag, and a bag pulls a ship sideways.
I closed her up by torchlight, on wood that had not finished moving. She will open somewhere. I do not yet know where, and that is what I mind.
She will swim. I think she will swim. She will need bailing every watch and mending every winter, and she will wet whatever lies lowest in her.
Or give me a month and sixty pennies. I take out what is worst and put in what is right. Then I will launch her gladly. Today I launch her because you pay me.
Pay the wright and launch her as she is
Give him a month and sixty pennies to put it right
Not yet: leave her on the slip

She goes down the rollers and floats. Water stands in her by evening, a hand deep, and no deeper by morning. The wright takes his silver and does not come to the ale. The house has a keel ship, and a bailer that will never be dry.

She goes down the rollers, floats, and by dark has filled to the thwarts at her post. It takes a day and a night and every man on the dam to get her dry and stop the seam. The house has a keel ship. Dorestad will not let you forget which one.
The wright has three strakes off her by nightfall, and he is whistling. A month, he says. Come back when the tar is dry and she will be a ship he can stand beside.
She stays on the rollers under her tar. The wright says she will not get better by standing there, and she will not get worse.
The long ship on the Rhine

She is on the rollers, and nothing else on the Rhine looks like her: long, low, sixteen oar ports, her stems a man's height above the rail. Half Dorestad has come to see whether she floats. The other half has come to see what the count's men say.
Sixteen oars and twelve men. You will curse the bread they eat. Then one day something will come over the edge of the sea behind you, and you will bless every mouth.
I have built ships for thirty winters, and this winter I learned something. Do not tell the Dane. He knows it already.
Your toll man came down yesterday and asked whether she was built for the Danish king. I said she was built for a man who dislikes being late.
Think how she looks from a dune. Every watchman on this coast will light his fire when he sees those stems. Hang something Christian where it shows.
She is thin, and thin forgives nothing. With that wood and that iron I would not take her past the river mouth before her first winter's mending. I will not steer her.
My skipper sails for Ripa without me if I ask him. A ship like this wants a man at the steering oar who has stood at one. I have. I know the way in to Ripa in the dark.
Bend on the sail, pay the wright, and ask the Dane to steer her
Pay the wright and launch her
Not yet: leave her on the slip

She slides in and hardly marks the water. The Dane takes the steering oar as a man takes his own cup, and gives you a riddle of his people for luck. With the grey sail up she goes down the river faster than a man can ride the bank. A Frisian wright has built a northern ship at Dorestad, and the Dane will show you the way in to Ripa.

She slides in and hardly marks the water. Your men sit down to sixteen oars and look at one another. The Dane watches from the dam and goes back to his own ship. The house has a long ship, and Dorestad has something to talk about until harvest.
She stays on the rollers. Boys come at dusk to count her oar ports and always make it a different number.
The river ship

On the bank below the old fort lies the great oak, hollowed thin as a shield, spread wide over a slow fire and raised with two strakes pegged with willow. There is not a nail in her. A short mast stands well forward for the tow rope.
One tree, forty-six feet of it. I hollowed her to two fingers and opened her over the fire like a pod. If she cracks, she cracks then. She did not.
The estate's wine goes down the river at Martinmas, and cloaks come up for the household. I would sooner send it in a ship I watched being made.
The emperor has said no new tolls where men only stretch a rope across the water. Some lords along this river have not heard yet. Carry my word and they hear quicker.
Half a pound to the wright and she is yours. Take the estate's carrying with her, and three casks go aboard today on account.
Upstream you haul her by rope from the bank, as everyone does. And at Saint Goar's cell you stop and say the prayer. Frisians have passed it by. The river remembers them.
Pay the wright and take the estate's carrying
Pay the wright and owe the estate nothing
Leave her on the bank until you have the silver

She floats in a hand's depth of water and three casks hardly move her. The steward's boatman shows you the channel as far as the first bend, and tells you the rest as you go. Sixteen bolts of Frisian cloaks are wanted here before the spring, well over the price. The house has turned to the river.
She floats in a hand's depth of water. The steward wishes you a good river and gives his wine to another boat. The house has a river ship and owes nobody for her.
She lies on the bank under wet sacking so that she does not dry and crack. The wright will keep her so for fifteen days. He mentions that sacking is not free.
The ship on the penny
The moneyer's bench in the upper town is bright with new pennies. On one side stands the emperor's name. On the other, where the old dies had a cross or an axe, there is a ship.
New dies, and the name of the town round a ship. A mast, a yard, a steering oar, and stems that turn up. I needed something to look at while I cut it.
I sat two mornings on your dam with a wax tablet. She holds still better than most. If the mast is a little short, that is my hand, not your wright's.
I sat on your dam with a wax tablet. I left out the man bailing. A die has only so much room.
I began with yours. The count's steward looked at the wax and asked whether the emperor's penny was to carry a Danish ship. So the stems came down a little. Hers are still in it, if you know.
When I was a boy, Dorestad's penny had an axe on it. Nobody ever told me whose axe. A ship, at least, everyone here understands.
Give him two worn pennies for the first one struck, and keep it
Ask for it as a gift between neighbours
A penny is a penny
He finds the first one struck, a little off its centre, and takes two worn ones for it. You put it where it will not be spent. An heir will ask one day what ship that is.
He turns the first one over twice and gives it to you, off its centre as it is. Between neighbours, he says, and writes nothing down. You put it where it will not be spent.
You take your change in ships and spend them at the dams before evening. They buy what any penny buys.
At Dorestad the wright at the dam heads has a keel ship on order for one of the small houses. He has been paid in earnest and is cheerful, which is noticed.
A raft of Rhineland oak came down to the dam heads at Dorestad, and a new keel is laid there: thirty-four feet, for a sea-going trader.
A Frisian house at Dorestad gave its new ship to the count for the king's service before she had touched water. The count counted the cost back, and more.
A new keel ship went down the rollers at Dorestad's dam heads and swims. She carries six tons, and the priest of the upper church blessed her.
A Frisian wright at Dorestad has built a ship in the Danish manner, long and low with sixteen oars, for a house of the town. A Dane lined her off. The count's men have been to look.
At Colonia a Frisian house has had a river ship made of one great oak from the king's wood, with no iron in her, and has taken to the river trade.

A late-summer afternoon at Dorestad's dam heads, low sun. In front, an empty slip of sand and blocks, and a broad Frisian wright of about fifty cutting notches in a hazel stick; behind him the player's small four-oared boat, deep in the water at a post, and the long row of timber dams.

An autumn morning in an oak wood across the Rhine from Colonia, mist between the trunks. A Frankish steward in a belted tunic and short cloak lays his hand on one enormous oak; the merchant beside him holds the notched stick. Far behind, the old stone fort and the river.

A grey cold day at the dam head. A raft of oak trunks bound with withies lies low in the water with a Frank asleep on it under his cloak; the wright stands on it with the back of his axe raised to strike a trunk, his head tilted to listen. On the sand behind, men drive wedges into a trunk that is splitting along its length.

The IJssel bank at Daventre under a sky smudged with smoke from the heath to the west. A smith with a leather apron and burnt forearms holds the notched stick against a rivet; ten small kegs stand in a row by his door, and men with yokes come down a sandy track carrying dark lumps of iron.

Inside a sunken hut on the terp at Wijnaldum, dim, lit from the door. An upright loom leans on the wall with its rows of clay weights hanging; a Frisian woman of about forty in a wool dress and head-cloth stands before it looking at her own hands. Through the door, sheep on the green mound and flat grey marsh.

The largest weaving hut, winter light. A great grey wool sail lies folded on a bench, thick as a mattress, its seams showing; the weaver holds a red thread full of knots. Four other women stand along the wall with their arms folded, watching the merchant.

A frosty morning on the slip. The new ship is a keel, two tall stems and three strakes a side, held by props. A lean Dane in a shaggy cloak, a hammer amulet at his neck, points along the keel with his whole arm; the Frisian wright faces him with his adze over his shoulder; the wright's men have stopped work to listen.

Midwinter dusk at the slip, snow on the dams. The hull has four strakes a side and nobody working on her. The wright sits on an upturned keg with his hands on his knees, immovable; beside him a single plank is clamped to the hull, waiting. The merchant stands before him with his breath showing.

A bright cold noon. A Frankish count in a fur-edged cloak, sword at his hip, stands before the half-planked hull with his thumbs in his belt; behind him his steward holds two horses. The wright's men are all crowded at the far stem, very busy. The merchant stands alone between the count and the ship.

An early spring morning, clear, the river high. The finished ship stands tarred black on tallowed rollers with her stem to the water and a grey sail furled on her yard. A priest in a white alb reads from a small book; the wright has one hand flat on her planks; a line of townspeople hold the ropes. The old small boat lies at a post beside her.

A dull day with rain coming. The ship is on the rollers, tarred and whole to look at. The wright stands under her stem with his arms folded and his knife still in his belt, looking at one seam; a boy beside him holds a wooden bailer. Few people have come to watch.

A windy spring day at the dam heads. A long, low ship with sixteen oar ports and stems rising a man's height stands on the rollers among the broad Frisian hulls. The Dane stands at her stern with his hand on the steering oar; the wright looks along her side; a crowd lines the dams, and two of the count's spearmen stand apart, watching.

The river bank below the old fort across from Colonia, late winter, thin sun. A very long, narrow, shallow boat made of one hollowed oak with two pegged strakes lies on the shingle, a short mast far forward; the embers of a long fire smoke beside her. A wright with an adze and the steward stand at her bow; three casks wait on the bank, and the towers of the city show over the water.

The moneyer's bench in the upper town of Dorestad, morning light through a shutter. In front, a spill of bright new silver pennies on a board, each with a small ship on it; an ageing Frankish moneyer holds one up between finger and thumb. Beside him lie a hammer, an iron die and a wax tablet scratched with the outline of a ship.
